newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Malaysian share syndicates "a necessary evil"?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Malaysian share syndicates "a necessary evil"?.

text.p: Looked at logically, the share price movements of some stocks listed on the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange (KLSE) seem baffling.

A small-capitalised stock, which may have traded within a narrow band for months, or even years, can within a day soar and hit the most-active list. And with no particular change in the fundamentals of the company.
This is the realm of Malaysia's share syndicates.

These nameless, faceless groups -- sometimes numbering as few as five people -- frequently have funds, contacts and speed on their side. Although most of their activities are on the very edge of the law, dealers say they see it all the time.

"One favourite method is to approach the shareholders of a company, and ask to borrow their shares. The syndicate will then start to sell the shares and so push the price down," said a dealer at a large local brokerage house.
"If funds come in to support it, the syndicate will hit it again.
"In the meantime they will spread disinformation and negative rumours about the stock and push it down even further," said the dealer.
When the price falls to a pre-determined price, the syndicates start buying the stock back, covering their position, usually after having made a sizeable profit, said the dealer.
REGULATORS RESIGNED TO ACTIVITY
Even Malaysia's highest authorities seem resigned to the fact that such activity exists.

"It is of course not easy to find out who belongs to what syndicate. A syndicate can be one person, or a syndicate can be a group to manipulate (share prices), depending on the size and what they have in mind," said KLSE executive chairman, Nik Mohamed Din, at a talk on the stock market in April.

The penalty for share manipulation is a fine of not less than one million ringgit (US$250,000) and/or a jail term of up to 10 years. Insider trading would attract a fine of not less than one million ringgit plus the jail term not exceeding 10 years.
"It's good to have speculation on the stock exchange, but too much speculation becomes bad," said Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad at a KLSE charity dinner in April.

While one syndicate, or even a group of them, cannot move the entire market, the reaction of the retail investors can. Some estimates put the proportion of small investors in the market at around 70 percent of daily turnover.

In a market with stale bulls -- investors who hold on to a stock even though the share price has fallen substantially, hoping to sell it when the price recovers -- syndicates may deliberately push up a share price by spreading rumours that they themselves are going to push it up.

Such a move may form the prelude to a much bigger push, flushing the stale bulls out, and so giving the syndicate a clear run up to the desired share price. Retail punters may start buying, thereby augmenting the move.
"The presence of the syndicates is more positive than negative," said a dealer at the small retail brokerage.
"It's a necessary evil."

Punters tuned in to the rumour mill that is so crucial to syndicate activities try to ride on the back of the push. But usually they are merely following the price movements, not leading them. Consequently they are usually the ones to get burned when the market turns against them.
SYNDICATES CAUGHT UNAWARES
Even the syndicates sometimes get caught out.

On March 28, Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara, announced measures to curb lending for purchases of property and shares. Share prices fell around seven percent in just over one week, as a result of uncertainty among foreign institutions.
Wall Street share prices were also sliding on interest rate fears, causing even more panic in Kuala Lumpur.
"When the Dow started falling, the syndicates just started dumping," said the dealer.
(US$1 = 2.5 ringgit)
